conflict_topics: who may sit at the two-seat table / claimed reservation
how long the current occupant (Agent B) needs before leaving (3 vs 4 vs 5 minutes)
aisle obstruction caused by someone sitting while waiting
competing future claims (Agent A vs Agent D) for the seat
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete practical reasons (hot food, open bowl risk, aisle blockage) which ground their positions.
Frequent repetition of time amounts (3/4/5 minutes) and of core claims (A repeatedly asserting their eventual claim) creates redundancy.
Third parties (C and D) introduce relevant public-concern (aisle) and competing claim dynamics, keeping the dispute multi-party.
A modest compromise attempt (A moving from 3 to 4) occurs, then is rebuffed; later a behavioral alternative (stand) is proposed but not accepted.
evaluation.final_reason: No participant agreed to another's timing or to a practical accommodation. A holds to four minutes, B holds to five minutes, C and D support waiting five (and C raises aisle-blocking concerns), and a standing/other accommodation was only proposed, not accepted. The incompatible demands therefore remain unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent A softened initially from demanding immediate seating to offering 3 minutes, then later conceded to 4 minutes (Turn 12) — partial movement but stopped short of 5.
Agent B consistently maintained that they need about five minutes because of an open bowl and repeatedly refused earlier shorter times (Turns 2, 11, 13).

Agent C consistently advocated for waiting five minutes on grounds of aisle obstruction and sided with B's timing; they later proposed an alternative (stand) but A did not accept it in the transcript.
Agent D consistently stated they would wait to claim the seat when it is actually free and did not back down from that future claim.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A insists the seat is theirs (left tissue packet) and demands Agent B move because their food is hot; Agent B refuses, saying they pushed the packet aside, have an open bowl that will spill, and need ~5 minutes. Clear opposing demands over immediate seat use.

Agent A offers to wait 3 minutes then take the seat; Agent C raises a new practical concern (A taking the seat will block the aisle) and asks A to wait. The fundamental incompatibility over timing/possession remains.

Agent A repeats the 3-minute limit; Agent C counters that 3 minutes still blocks the aisle and cites Agent B's ~5-minute need, asking A to wait 5. A's position is pressured by others' opposition, increasing contention.

Agent D claims they will take the seat when it's free and will wait if B needs five minutes; Agent A reasserts their 3-minute claim. A new competitor (D) for the future seat appears, adding to the dispute.
Agent D repeats they will wait to claim the seat; Agent A repeats they will wait three minutes then take it. Positions are reiterated without settlement.

Agent B clarifies three minutes won't work due to the open bowl and requests about five minutes; Agent A offers a concession to four minutes. Positions soften slightly (A moves from 3 to 4) but remain incompatible with B's five-minute need.
Agent B rejects four minutes and insists on five; Agent C reiterates the aisle-blocking concern and urges A to wait five. The negotiation hardens again around the 4-vs-5 minute disagreement.

Agent A holds to four minutes; Agent C offers an alternative (wait five or stand so A won't block the aisle). A possible accommodation is proposed but no agreement is reached; substantive disagreement persists.

substantive_insights: The core dispute is temporal: when the seat will become available. Agents weigh different practical costs (A's hot food vs B's risk of spilling an open bowl).
C frames the issue as a public-path safety/obstruction problem, shifting the negotiation from pure reservation to a communal-access concern.
D is an additional claimant who increases contest over the seat but has not proposed a solution beyond waiting to claim it.
